source.title: Neural scaling of deep chemical models
source.authors: Nathan C Frey; Ryan Soklaski; Simon Axelrod; Siddharth Samsi; Rafael Gómez-Bombarelli; Connor W. Coley; V. Gadepally

record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling in chemical language models and neural force fields, and reports resolution-limited breakdowns and dataset-dependent power-law regimes that qualify a single general scaling law.
record.gate_note: The study reports held-out loss scaling results for ChemGPT and GNN force-field models. Its training-performance-estimation results predict final loss from early training speed; they do not test whether scaling fits on small models extrapolate to much larger models, so those results are not rows for V2.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws to held-out loss against model and data size in two non-text settings: chemical-string LMs (ChemGPT on SELFIES) and GNN force fields. That is a new-setting test of V5. It also bears on V7, because the exponent and the power-law range shift with dataset size and architecture. It does not test text LMs, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, shape at fixed parameters or downstream tasks.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors claim to discover empirical power-law neural-scaling relations for chemical LMs (β=0.17 on the largest dataset) and equivariant GNN force fields (β=0.26). They report that loss is not saturated with model size, data or compute. Power-law regimes are dataset-dependent and break down when resolution-limited. They frame the results as guidance for allocating resources, not as a fitted compute-optimal law.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses chemical-string language models and molecular force-field GNNs, with held-out cross-entropy or force L1 loss and domain-specific datasets. It does not reproduce the original text-language-model scaling experiments or fixed-compute allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: ChemGPT power-law regimes and fitted exponents vary with dataset size; the largest-dataset fit omits the three largest models. GNN scaling exponents vary by architecture, with the equivariant models reported as more sample-efficient than SchNet.

fits_no_version.finding: Equivariant GNNs (PaiNN, Allegro) show larger data-scaling exponents than invariant SchNet at fixed capacity c=64.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural inductive biases (equivariance) change the data-scaling exponent, not only the loss offset.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimal GNN capacity and depth-versus-width split depend on dataset size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal model shape depends on data scale in GNN force fields.

record.code_released: LitMatter repository on GitHub (URL not stated in the text)
record.problems: ChemGPT models were trained for a fixed 10 epochs for computational reasons, and hyperparameters were held fixed across model and dataset sizes although the authors state optimal settings may change. Scaling fits are approximate and the largest-dataset fit excludes the three largest models. No repeated trials are reported for the scaling experiments. For GNNs, validation data include seen chemical species, and the authors note that capacity trends may partly reflect memorization or random initialization. Several GNN exponent values are only in supplementary material not included in the provided text.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported loss-scaling outcomes were left out. The TPE early-training prediction results in Figs. 2–3 and Table 1 were excluded because they predict final loss from training speed rather than test scaling-law extrapolation.

untested.parts: Text language models are not studied. ChemGPT is a chemical-string model and is treated under V5. No compute power law is reported.
All of it. Training performance estimation (TPE) predicts final loss from early training, not large runs from small-run fits.
All of it. There is no fixed-compute allocation analysis.
There is no comparison at fixed parameter count. GNN depth versus width is mentioned only qualitatively.
Image and video models, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested. No compute scaling is reported.
All of it. Only pretraining and validation loss are measured.
Parameter-counting conventions, training schedule and fitting method are not varied.

record.verdict_notes: The tranche changes from T5 to T3: this is a new-setting test, and the breakdowns are reported qualitatively rather than argued as a refutation. ChemGPT was trained for a fixed 10 epochs (not converged) with hyperparameters fixed across sizes, and there were no repeated trials. Both factors could distort exponents. 'Model size' for the GNNs is capacity (depth × width), not parameter count. The training performance estimation (TPE) results are correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests chemical language models, not ordinary text language models; it does not test a general law across all language models or report a compute-scaling power law for ChemGPT.
No power-law fit on small runs is used to predict loss on runs orders of magnitude larger. Early-training performance estimation is a different prediction procedure.
The study does not compare parameter/token allocations at fixed compute or fit compute-optimal parameter and token trends.
GNN depth and width are varied, but the study does not compare architecture details at a fixed parameter count to test whether they change loss only slightly.
The study tests chemical-string pretraining and molecular force prediction, not image or video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study evaluates pretraining or validation loss, not downstream task performance or its predictability.

The study does not test dependence on alternative parameter-count conventions, training schedules, or fitting methods; it does report dataset-dependent regimes, fit exclusions, and power-law breakdowns.

rows.subject: ChemGPT
rows.size_stated: 77,600 to 1,208,455,168 non-embedding parameters; fit range 10^5 to 10^7 non-embedding parameters
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size and measured cross-entropy on a fixed held-out validation set.

conditions.value: largest dataset considered; up to 10 million molecules and 300 million tokens

rows.measure: Held-out causal-language-model cross-entropy; fitted model-size scaling exponent β.
rows.value: β = 0.17 ± 0.01; the three largest models were discarded from the power-law fit.
rows.locator: Results, “Neural scaling quantifies the improvements in loss”; Supplementary Fig. 1 (fit details referenced in text); Fig. 4
rows.note: The text reports approximate power-law scaling over the stated model-size range for the largest dataset. The three largest models were omitted from the fit.
rows.check: Not V1: SELFIES molecule strings are a non-text modality, so this belongs to V5. The power law spans only about 2 orders of magnitude (10^5–10^7) and the 3 largest models were dropped. Training was a fixed 10 epochs, not to convergence. Partial for V5; supports bending for V7.

rows.subject: ChemGPT
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size and measured cross-entropy on a fixed held-out validation set.
rows.measure: Held-out causal-language-model cross-entropy; fitted model-size scaling exponent β.
rows.locator: Results, “Neural scaling quantifies the improvements in loss”; Supplementary Fig. 2 (fit details referenced in text)
rows.note: The reported exponent differs from the largest-dataset fit, consistent with the authors’ statement that the scaling regime depends on dataset size.
rows.check: Remove V1 (non-text modality). The fit range for the next-largest dataset is not stated in the text. β=0.30 versus 0.17 shows the exponent depends on dataset size.

rows.subject: ChemGPT
rows.operation_detail: Varied training dataset size and measured held-out cross-entropy.
rows.measure: Held-out causal-language-model cross-entropy as dataset size increases.
rows.value: The loss improves monotonically with dataset size up to nearly 10 million molecules; the text reports no evidence of diminishing returns for the dataset sizes considered.
rows.locator: Results, “Neural scaling quantifies the improvements in loss”; Fig. 4
rows.note: This is an explicit monotonic-loss result, but the text does not give a fitted dataset-size exponent for ChemGPT.
rows.check: Only monotonic improvement with data is reported. No data-size power-law fit or exponent is given, so the power-law form cannot be read. V7 link dropped.

rows.subject: ChemGPT
rows.operation_detail: Compared held-out cross-entropy across model sizes at different dataset sizes.
rows.measure: Shape of held-out loss versus model size.
rows.value: Power-law-like regimes occur at different model-size ranges depending on dataset size; the smallest dataset shows such scaling between 10^7 and 10^8 parameters, while the largest dataset shows it between 10^5 and 10^7. Power-law scaling breaks down in resolution-limited regimes.
rows.locator: Results, “Neural scaling quantifies the improvements in loss”; Supplementary Figs. 1–2 referenced in text
rows.note: The authors describe the fits as approximate and the regimes as dataset-dependent; they characterize breakdowns as resolution-limited and cite broken power laws as a more general description.
rows.check: Remove V1. The text also reports saturation above 100M params on the largest dataset, and a plateau then improvement on the smallest dataset. Partial for V5; observed bending for V7.

rows.subject: PaiNN
rows.size_stated: GNNs with millions of trainable parameters; capacity varied using depth × width
rows.stage_stated: training on ANI-1x molecular geometries to predict atomic forces
rows.operation_detail: Varied dataset size and model capacity, then measured validation force loss.

conditions.value: 50,000 frames held out by random sampling

rows.measure: Validation force loss across dataset sizes and model capacities.
rows.value: Monotonic loss improvements with increasing dataset size; for fixed dataset size, converged loss was strongly correlated with model capacity and total training time. For datasets other than 10^3 datapoints, Spearman ρ ≥ 0.88 with capacity and ρ ≥ 0.75 with training time.
rows.locator: Results, “GNNs exhibit robust neural-scaling behaviour”; Fig. 5
rows.note: The dataset spans four orders of magnitude. The authors warn that the validation set shares chemical species with the training set and that capacity effects may partly reflect memorization.
rows.check: Reports monotonic loss with data and Spearman correlations with capacity and time, not a power-law fit. Seen-species validation may reflect memorisation (ρ≥0.93 at 10^4). No V7 content.

rows.subject: PaiNN
rows.size_stated: capacity varied by depth × width; GNNs with millions of trainable parameters
rows.stage_stated: training on ANI-1x molecular geometries to predict atomic forces

conditions.value: multiple orders of magnitude of dataset size

rows.measure: Dataset-size scaling exponent for validation loss.
rows.baseline: SchNet and Allegro at the same stated capacity
rows.value: PaiNN has a larger β scaling parameter than SchNet; numerical exponent not stated in the provided text.

rows.note: The authors report larger scaling exponents for equivariant GNNs and say the same trend remains when excluding the smallest and largest datasets from the fits.
rows.check: The exponent value is only in Supplementary Table 1. The abstract gives 0.26 for equivariant GNNs, which should be recorded.

relationships.condition: ChemGPT model-size scaling on the two largest PubChem datasets; GNN force fields across dataset sizes
relationships.reason: Approximate power laws with fitted exponents: β=0.17 and 0.30 for ChemGPT (C1, C2); fitted data exponents for PaiNN, Allegro and SchNet, with 0.26 for the equivariant models (G2–G4).
relationships.display_finding: ChemGPT model-size exponents were 0.17 and 0.30, while force-field data scaling followed fitted power laws with exponent 0.26 for the equivariant models.

relationships.condition: ChemGPT across the full model-size range, under fixed 10-epoch training
relationships.reason: The power law holds over only about 2 decades of model size. Loss saturates above 100M params or plateaus depending on dataset, and the 3 largest models were excluded from the fit (C1, C4).
relationships.display_finding: The power law held over approximately two orders of magnitude, while loss saturated above 100M parameters or plateaued depending on the dataset; the three largest models were excluded from fitting.

relationships.condition: ChemGPT across dataset sizes; GNNs across architectures
relationships.reason: The exponent shifts with dataset size (0.17 vs 0.30) and the power-law range moves, with breaks the authors call broken power laws (C1, C2, C4). GNN exponents differ by architecture (G2–G4).
relationships.display_finding: ChemGPT exponents change between 0.17 and 0.30 with dataset size and exhibit shifting power-law regions and breaks, while GNN exponents differ across architectures.
